primarySources.title: Linux kernel PWM interface
facts: The kernel API applies period, duty cycle, and enabled state together.
Consumers cannot rely on a disabled PWM producing a particular output state.
pwm_get_state reports the last requested state and may differ from what hardware implemented; it is not independent position feedback.
A later hardware adapter must use an appropriate selected driver and cannot infer motion from command state.

primarySources.title: Linux GPIO character-device v2 API
facts: The official documentation warns against userspace bit-banging when a proper subsystem driver exists and points to PWM/SPI/I2C subsystems.
GPIO edge events carry timestamps plus request-wide and per-line sequence numbers; the default clock is monotonic and not wall time.

primarySources.title: Linux GPIO v2 line event read
facts: Edge events are kernel-buffered and read in detection order.
Logical polarity can differ from physical polarity, so an eventual limit/interlock adapter needs an exact selected configuration and independent validation.

primarySources.title: Linux IIO buffers
facts: Buffered sensor data must be interpreted from scan metadata including endian, signedness, valid bits, storage bits, repetition, and shift.
A later physical feedback adapter must bind and validate the selected scan layout rather than assume a byte format.

primarySources.title: Linux IIO core elements
facts: IIO exposes an explicit device timestamp clock and timestamp acquisition.
A later physical adapter must retain source clock identity and supply an explicit mapping before source capture time can be compared with gateway time.

primarySources.title: Node.js timers
facts: Node makes no guarantee that a callback fires at the exact requested delay or in a guaranteed order.
The software fixture can test configuration, ordering, cancellation, and observed tolerances but cannot establish hard real-time slew/deadman behavior.
